titre: A Man Hidden Beneath Picasso's *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*)
accroche: Without the money for a new canvas, Picasso paints over a finished portrait. A century later, no one knows who it shows.
contenu_vulgarise:
*La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*), painted by Pablo Picasso in 1901, shows a woman bathing in a bluish interior, seen from behind, bent over a basin. The painting has belonged to the Phillips Collection in Washington since 1927. As early as 1954, a conservator at the museum notices something odd in the brushstrokes visible on the surface: lines that correspond to no shape in the painted composition.

It is not until the 1990s that a first X-ray confirms that a motif really does lie hidden beneath the visible layer of paint, though no one can yet say which.

## A Face Beneath the Color

The museum relaunches the investigation in 2007, when the curator Patricia Favero resumes the study of the painting. In 2008, an infrared camera fitted with a spectral filter set to a specific wavelength this time penetrates the blue paint layer with unprecedented clarity: it reveals the face and torso of a bearded man, in a jacket and bow tie, his head resting on his hand, three rings on his fingers.

The investigation intensifies again in 2012. Teams from the National Gallery of Art, Cornell University and the Winterthur Museum join the Phillips Collection to analyze the painting by X-ray fluorescence, a method that identifies the chemical elements of pigments, layer by layer, without touching the paint. The analyses show that the pigments of the two compositions are identical, which strengthens the hypothesis that both are indeed by Picasso's hand. Examination of paint cross-sections under the microscope also suggests that Picasso painted one over the other once the first layer was already largely dry, perhaps only three or four months apart.

The reason for this recycling, for its part, is hardly mysterious. Picasso is twenty, living in Paris with no money, and a new canvas is expensive. A museum curator, Susan Behrends Frank, sums it up simply: when he had an idea, he had to carry it out, and he couldn't afford to buy a canvas every time; he sometimes even painted on cardboard, which was cheaper than canvas.

## A Name Still Missing

One question remains that science has not resolved: who is this man? Researchers have ruled out the hypothesis of a self-portrait. One name circulates, that of the Parisian art dealer Ambroise Vollard, who organizes Picasso's first solo exhibition in Paris in 1901; but no document, no clue left on the canvas allows it to be confirmed.

What *La Chambre bleue* reveals thus goes beyond a mere technical feat. An X-ray does not restore an identity: it makes visible a shape, a face, a posture, not the name of the person who bears them. The hidden portrait became legible again in 2014, after half a century of one conservator's hesitation, two decades of imprecise X-rays and six years of cross-analysis among four institutions. It remains, to this day, anonymous.

repere.texte: X-ray and infrared examinations carried out in the 1990s hint at a hidden composition, without a clear image. The curator Patricia Favero resumes the study of the painting in 2007. In 2012, four institutions (Phillips Collection, National Gallery of Art, Cornell University, Winterthur Museum) analyze the painting by X-ray fluorescence.

carte.punch: Without the money for a new canvas, Picasso paints *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*) over a portrait of a man.
carte.idee: Beneath Picasso's *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*, 1901) lies the portrait of a bearded man in a bow tie, discovered by X-ray and then infrared imaging between the 1990s and 2014. His identity remains unknown to this day.

quiz.question: How do researchers confirm the presence and dating of the portrait hidden beneath *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*)?
choix: By comparing Picasso's signature to the one found on other canvases painted in Paris during his Blue Period, between 1901 and 1904
By finding, in the Phillips Collection's archives, a letter in which Picasso himself describes the painting he covered over
By cross-referencing infrared imaging, which reveals a face beneath the painted layer, with a pigment analysis confirming the same period
By questioning the descendants of the Parisian art dealer Ambroise Vollard about a portrait that has since disappeared
quiz.explication: Infrared imaging, from 2008, reveals the face and torso of a man beneath the blue layer; pigment analysis by X-ray fluorescence, from 2012, confirms that the two compositions share the same palette. No compared signature, no archival letter and no questioned descendant figure in this demonstration.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Since what year has the Phillips Collection owned *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*)?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The painting has belonged to the museum since 1927, as the entry states; 1901 is the year it was created, 1954 the year of a conservator's first remark, 2008 the year of the infrared imaging.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Picasso paint *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*) over an already finished portrait?
choix: He considered his first portrait a failure and wanted to start over
The sitter had asked for his portrait to be erased
He lacked the money to buy a new canvas
The original canvas had been damaged by the damp in his studio
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the entry, Picasso was twenty, living in Paris with no money, and a new canvas was expensive; he sometimes even painted on cardboard, which was cheaper.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What name is put forward, without proof to confirm it, for the man hidden beneath *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*)?
choix: Guillaume Apollinaire, poet and art critic
Max Jacob, friend and roommate of Picasso
An anonymous client of Picasso's studio
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The name of Ambroise Vollard, who organizes Picasso's first solo exhibition in Paris in 1901, circulates without any document confirming it.
